meaning: an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas

phonemes.desc: A short open a, tapped r, and the breathy voiced ɦ — the root √arh, 'to deserve,' announcing itself in the first syllable.
A light dental t closing the present-participle ending — arhat, 'the deserving one,' worthiness as a grammatical form.

pronunciation.approximation: 'UHR-hut' — short vowels throughout; the h is a voiced breath between the syllables, and the final t is pure dental, not English 't'.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: √arh 'to deserve, to be worthy' + present-participle -at — arhat, 'the worthy one' (Monier-Williams)

kin.label: Pāli
kin.form: arahant — the canonical title the Buddha applies to himself: arahaṃ sammāsambuddho

kin.label: Jaina Prakrit
kin.form: arahanta — the Jinas are 'worthy ones,' parallel title in the sister śramaṇa tradition (Ācārāṅga Sūtra)

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Arhat' is ASCII-canonical, with nothing lost in plain spelling; the restoration's weight is semantic — the title literally means 'worthy of gifts,' holiness as a completed and inspectable task.

domains.title: Arhat
domains.subtitle: The Worthy One — Perfection as a Finished Task
domains.lead: The arhat is the ideal of early Buddhism made flesh: one who has destroyed the taints, done what had to be done, and laid down the burden — freedom achieved in this life, by this person, without a god's intervention. The Theragāthā lets the finished saints speak for themselves.

cards.name: Worthy of Gifts
cards.desc: The literal sense — āhūneyyo, 'worthy of offerings,' the field of merit for gods and men alike.

cards.name: The Task Complete
cards.desc: The canonical formula: 'done is what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the goal' — the end of need itself.

cards.name: The Four Stages
cards.desc: Stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat — the graduated ladder to the deathless, rung by rung.

cards.name: The Sixteen Lohans
cards.desc: In China the arhat ideal became an immortal garrison — sixteen great disciples commanded to guard the Dharma until Maitreya comes.

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The arhat's only possession — and the reason the laity feed him: the worthy one is a field of merit, and a donation ripens

symbols.name: The crutch and long eyebrows
symbols.meaning: The lohans' immortal attributes in Chinese art — longevity so extreme it needs support, and sight so deep it overgrows

symbols.name: The flame of the taints extinguished
symbols.meaning: Nirvāṇa as a fire gone out — the arhat is the one whose fuel (rāga, dosa, moha) is spent; nothing more burns

symbols.name: The lion's roar of assurance
symbols.meaning: The arhat's declaration 'there is no more coming to any state of being' — certainty spoken from completion, not faith

symbols.name: The assembly of elders
symbols.meaning: Sāriputta and Moggallāna flanking the Buddha — wisdom and powers as the twin pillars of the arhat ideal

mythology.lead: The arhat has no biography because the arhat is a hundred biographies — the finished saints of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, the chief disciples of the canon, and in China a band of sixteen immortals commanded to wait out the ages for the next Buddha.

myths.title: Worthy of Gifts
myths.text: Arhat comes from √arh, "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle -at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men. The Buddha claimed it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, "arahant, fully self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the Udāna records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded he prove it. The commentarial definition sharpens the word into a checklist: one who has destroyed the taints (āsava), lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, and knows "there is no more of this." The Jaina tradition uses the same word in parallel: its twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras are arhats, worthy ones who ford the flood of rebirth. The mythic weight of a title: Buddhism made holiness a completed task, not a birth — and gave it a word anyone could check.

myths.title: Sāriputta and Moggallāna
myths.text: The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in the Etadagga verses (AN 1): Sāriputta, foremost in great wisdom — the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the Sāriputta Sutta (SN 47.19), replied only that there was nowhere he had ever clung; and Moggallāna, foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, Kevaṭṭa Sutta). Both were murdered — Moggallāna beaten to death by brigands — the Buddha predicting that the pair would die as the twin sāla trees fall. The Theragāthā lets the arahants speak in their own voices: "Cut down the whole forest of craving, not just one tree; from the jungle of craving, fear is born." The ideal is given a human face twice — the thinker and the wonder-worker — and both faces end in the one death arahants cannot refuse.

myths.title: Four Gates to the Deathless
myths.text: Arahantship is the fourth and last gate. The canon maps the road precisely: the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), certain of awakening, never again reborn lower than human; the once-returner (sakadāgāmin), who comes back once to this world; the non-returner (anāgāmin), who awakens in a higher heaven and does not return at all; and the arahant, freed here and now. The decisive faculty is stated everywhere and nowhere better than the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10): mindfulness of body, feelings, mind, and dhammas — "the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow." Fifteen centuries later Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga (5th c. CE) welded the whole road into one manual, still the map of Theravāda practice. The interpretive core: holiness is gradual, inspectable, and irreversible — a ladder whose rungs can be named, and whose top rung is the end of needing anything, forever.

myths.title: The Lohans Who Guard the Dharma
myths.text: Chinese Buddhism gave the arahants a second life as luohan — sixteen great disciples the Buddha, before his parinirvāṇa, commanded to remain in the world without entering final nirvāṇa until Maitreya comes. Their charter text, Xuanzang's 654 translation of Nandimitra's Record of the Duration of the Dharma, names them — Mahākāśyapa, Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya, Kanakavatsa, Subhūti, Nandimitra himself and the rest — each assigned a mountain, a retinue, and a district of the earth to protect. The painter Guanxiu (10th c.) gave them their immortal faces, gaunt and strange, and his line was copied for a thousand years; Ming temples house ranks of gilded lohans, five hundred strong, each with his own demon, dragon, or tiger. The myth is a quiet reversal: the extinct ideal of early Buddhism — the saint who is done — is drafted as a permanent garrison, waiting out the ages at their posts for the next Buddha, deathless on duty.

lore.syncretism: The Jaina sister-tradition used the same title in parallel: every tīrthaṅkara is an arhat, and the two śramaṇa movements argued over who deserved the word — evidence that it belonged to the age, not to one sect. Mahāyāna sūtras, building the rival bodhisattva ideal, chastised the arhat's "selfish" release (the Lotus Sūtra likens the arhat vehicle to a burning house escaped too soon), yet kept the title for the Buddha himself and for Śāriputra, whose "future Buddhahood" the Lotus explicitly prophesies. In China the arhat became the lohan — an immortal in Taoist dress — and in Tibet the great arhats of the canon were painted as the Buddha's original saṅgha, the lineage every ordination renews. Modern vipassanā movements restored the word to practice: the arhat is again a goal, not a museum piece.
lore.culturalLegacy: The arhat's afterlife is the afterlife of the Theragāthā — a book of verses by the first saints, still chanted in Pāli lands, among the oldest autobiographies in the world. Chinese temples fill halls with lohan: the Five Hundred Arhats of Beijing's Biyun Si and the sixteen of Hangzhou's Jingshan Si are national treasures; Guanxiu's originals survive in Japan, designated national treasures there too. In Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia the arhat remains the living summit of the path — every forest monastery's kammaṭṭhāna tradition claims the title's ladder, rung by rung. And in the modern West, where "saint" had grown vague, "arhat" arrived with its etymology intact: the worthy one — holiness defined as a task you can finish.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The arhat is the most austere ideal any major religion has proposed: not love, not justice, not obedience — completion. The canonical formula is brutal in its economy: done is what had to be done; there is no more of this. No god approves it, no history rewards it, no heaven awaits as payment. It is simply over.

That is why the Mahāyāna found it both admirable and insufficient, and why modern readers find it quietly devastating. The arhat does not save the world; the arhat leaves. Yet the tradition kept the begging bowl — the one object that binds the finished saint back to the unfinished crowd, who must feed him and so plant their own merit. Perfection, the bowl insists, is not private. The worthy one stands at the door precisely so that someone else can practice giving. The ideal of having nothing, it turns out, was always also a technology of connection.

sources.name: Nandimitra, Record of the Duration of the Dharma (Xuanzang trans., 654)

lore.archaeology: The arhat's archaeology is the archaeology of the aniconic saṅgha. The Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs (2nd–1st c. BCE) show the great disciples flanking the empty throne — identifiable by label in Brahmi inscriptions: Sāriputa, Mogalāna, Maha Kāsava. The earliest anthropomorphic saṅgha images come from Gandhāra and Mathurā (1st–3rd c. CE): monks in patched robes, each with his attribute. The lohans' gallery in Chinese art is documented from the Tang — Guanxiu's sixteen (c. 891–901) survive in the Tokyo Seikado and Imperial Household collections — and the Five Hundred Lohans halls of the Song and Ming (Jingshan, Biyun, Baoguang monasteries) preserve the type at monumental scale. In Pāli lands, the arhat leaves no relic-cults of his own by design: the finished one, the tradition says, leaves nothing to enshrine but the teaching.
